lawyer:
SS Halder, Senior, Advocate, instructed by Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record — For the Appellant. 
SM Ziaul Haque Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent No.1. 
Not represented — Respondent Nos. 2 & 3.
parties:
Shamsun Nahar Begum ------ Appellant
Vs.
Salauddin Ahmed and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: This appeal by leave at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant is against the judgment and order dated 9-7-95 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 3744 of 1995 affirming the judgment and order dated 20-5-95 passed by the Assistant Judge. 1st Court, Dhaka in Misc. Case No. 60 of 1991 under Order 9 rule 13 CPC allowing the said Misc. Case and setting aside the ex parte decree dated 25-4-85 and restoring original Title Suit No. 257 of 1994 to its file and number. 

 2. The plaintiff-appellant filed Title Suit No. 257 of 1994 in the Court of Assistant Judge, First Court Dhaka for specific performance of contract. The suit was decreed ex parte on 25-4-85. Against that ex parte judgment and decree defendant respondent filed on 25-9-91 Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1991 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff by suppression of all notices obtained the ex parte decree on 25-4-85, which he came to know by filing information slip on 23-4-91 through an Advocate, Shunil Ranjan Biswas; that thereafter by obtaining necessary papers he filed the case and that no summons was served upon him and the report of the serving peon is false. 

 3. Plaintiff appellant contested the Miscellaneous Case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that after taking the entire proposed money the agreement for sale was executed on 14-2-70 and possession was handed over along with the lease deed of the Housing Estate and all other documents; that thereafter another agreement was executed on 8-10-77; that the plaintiff was residing in the said house all through; that notice was served in the original suit as well as at the time of registration of the document; that the defendant had full knowledge about the construction of the building and the living of the tenants; that the alleged knowledge dated 23-4-91 is absolutely false and the application is liable, to be dismissed; that the information slip stands in the name of one Shahabuddin Ahmed and not in the name of defendant No. 1. Plaintiff further asserted that the plaintiff's name has been duly mutated in the office of the Housing Estate, Ministry of Works, Municipality, WASA, WAPDA, Titas Gas, etc. and due notices were served upon defendant No. 1 for those mutation proceedings. The defendant had full prior knowledge of the decree and the pucca construction and, as such, the Miscellaneous case that was filed long after six years without any application for condemnation of delay is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that there was no due service of summons upon defendant No. 1 and consequently affirmed the order of the trial Court allowing the miscellaneous case under Order9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 (1) The ex parte decree was passed on 25-4-85 and the Miscellaneous case for setting aside the ex parte decree was filed on 25-5-91 long after six years without any explanation for condemnation of delay. 

 (3) The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not also consider that summons and registered notices were duly served upon the defendants and, as such, the learned Judge wrongly affirmed the order of the trial Court allowing the Miscellaneous Case for setting aside the ex parte decree. 

 (4) The defendant respondent having not examined any witness to prove his definite date of knowledge of the ex parte decree, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in allowing the application for setting aside the ex parte decree when the Miscellaneous Case was admittedly filed after six years. 

 7. From the order sheet it appears that the suit was filed on 25-4-84. From Order No. 8 dated 24-11-84 it appears that summons upon defendant No. 1 returned duly served as per peon's report and summons on defendant Nos. 2 and 3 did not return after service. Plaintiff also filed postal requisites and the court ordered for issuance of the same by registered post. From order No. 9 dated 10-12-84 it appears that acknowledgment due did not return by that time. From order No. 10 it appears that the court on 18-12-84 found that summons has been duly served and defendants filed no written statement. Next date was fixed for filing written statement and the defendants did not file any written statement and the case was fixed for ex parte hearing on 5-1-85. From 5-1-85 to 25-4-85 the defendant did not appear nor file any written statement nor took any steps. Ultimately, the suit was decreed ex parte on 25-4-85. 

 8. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found fault with the service of summons as the acknowledgment due was not received by the court and nothing was known about the said acknowledgment receipt. The learned Single Judge also found fault with the court for giving the declaration that summons has been served. The learned Single Judge further found fault for fixing the case on 26-11-84 for ex parte hearing without affording the defendants the statutory period of two months notice under Order 8 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure to file the written statement. From these above facts the learned Single Judge went on to hold that there was no due service of summons upon defendant No. 1. The report of the process server states that he has returned the summons and he also made a declaration to the effect that he served the summons by affixing the same on the door of defendant No. 1 under rule 17 as defendant No. 1 refused to receive the summons. The process server as a serving officer of the court has also given a declaration to the effect that he has served the same in the same manner as indicated in the report. 

 9. A reference to Order 5 rule 19 A of the Code of Civil Procedure shows that the declaration of the serving officer shall be received as evidence of the fact as to the service or attempted service of the summons. In the present case there was a declaration to the effect that the process server went to defendant No. 1's house with the summons but defendant No. 1 having refused to receive the same he served it by hanging on defendant No. 1's door in presence of three witnesses of the locality, namely, Shahed Ali, Azizuddin and Alauddin. In that view of the matter, the trial Court accepted such service as duly made under the law and the service of summons is to be construed as a valid service in law. 

 10. Mr SS Halder, learned Advocate for the appellant, cited the case of Santosh Kumar Chakraborty and others vs MA Motaleb Hossain and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 248 wherein the declaration of the process server was accepted by this court as evidence of that fact as to the service or attempted service of the summons. Mr SS Halder has also cited the case of Md Insan Ali vs Mir Abdus Sobhan, 40 DLR (AD) 193 to show, that there being declaration of the process-server as per rule 19A of Order 5 of the Code, the onus is shifted to the defendant to prove that the summons was not served upon him. Apart from this, rule 19B(2) of Order 5 speaks that if the acknowledgment due is lost or mislaid or for any other reason has not been received by the court within 30 days from the date of posting of the letter the court issuing the summons shall declare that the summons has been duly served on the defendant. In that view of the matter, the postal acknowledgment due in respect of service upon defendant Nos. 2 and 3 having not returned within 30 days there was no legal bar on the part of the court to proceed with the case after holding that the summons has been duly served on the said defendants. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was not correct in holding that the suit could not be fixed for ex parte hearing without return of the acknowledgment due. It further appears from the order sheet that on 18-12-84 the court made a declaration that the summons has been duly served and the suit was decreed ex parte on 25-4-85. So there was sufficient time for the defendants either to file a written statement or to take any steps for hearing. But no such step was taken by the defendants. As a matter of fact, ex parte hearing of the case was fixed on 26-12-84 and the ex parte decree was passed on 25-4-85, thereby more than two months time was afforded to the defendant-respondent to file a written statement or to take steps for the hearing of the suit. The materials on record show that there was valid and legal service. In view of the above finding by us, it is incumbent upon the defendants to show why the application for setting aside ex parte decree was filed long after six years of the ex parte decree and that too without any explanation of such long delay. We also find that Shahabuddin Ahmed through whom the defendant got his initial knowledge of the ex parte decree was not examined. The defendant did not examine any witness to prove his definite date of knowledge of the ex parte decree. As we find that summons and registered notices were validly and legally served upon the defendants it was the duty of the defendants to prove his initial date of knowledge of the ex parte decree. The defendants having failed to do so we hold that the defendant failed to prove his case. 

 For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and Miscellaneous Case No. 60 of 1991 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka is dismissed.
